title: What Happens to Your Stocks if Your Broker Shuts Down?
description: Understanding SIPC insurance and custodial segregation rules.
content:
When you log into Robinhood or Fidelity, you see numbers on a screen. But what if the website goes dark tomorrow? What if the brokerage goes bankrupt? After the collapse of FTX (Crypto) and Silicon Valley Bank, investors are rightfully worried about custodial risk. The good news is that the US stock market system is structurally different from crypto or banking. Your assets are segregated. This guide explains the safety nets—SIPC, Excess SIPC, and street name registration—that protect your life savings.

Key Takeaways

  • Asset Segregation: By US law (SEC Rule 15c3-3), brokers must keep client assets separate from company assets. If the broker goes bust, they cannot use your stocks to pay their debts.
  • SIPC Insurance: The Securities Investor Protection Corporation covers up to $500,000 per account type (including up to $250k cash) if assets are missing.
  • Not Market Insurance: SIPC protects against theft or broker failure. It does NOT protect against the value of your stocks going down. If you buy a bad stock, that's on you.
  • The Transfer Process: In 99% of broker failures, another broker buys the accounts. You wake up one day and your 'TD Ameritrade' login is now a 'Schwab' login. You lose nothing.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Unlike crypto exchanges where you are an 'unsecured creditor', US brokerage accounts have strict legal protections. You own the underlying shares (beneficially), not the broker.

The Safety Net Hierarchy

What actually happens in a disaster?

Layer 1: Segregation (The Wall)

Even if Robinhood owes billions, they cannot touch your VTI shares. Your shares are held at a depository (DTCC). In a bankruptcy, the trustee simply moves your record of ownership to a solvent broker.

Layer 2: SIPC (The Backstop)

If fraud occurs (e.g., Bernie Madoff scenario where the broker stole the shares), SIPC steps in.
Limit: $500,000 total per customer capacity ($250k cash limit).
Note: This limit applies per 'separate capacity' (Individual, Joint, Roth are separate).

Layer 3: Excess SIPC (The Bonus)

Big brokers (Fidelity, Schwab) buy private insurance on top of SIPC. This often covers up to $1 Billion in total losses. Check your broker's 'Account Protection' page for their specific policy.

How to Protect Yourself

  1. Split Large Balances: If you have $2 Million cash, don't keep it in one brokerage account (SIPC cash limit is $250k). Buy 'Cash Equivalents' like Money Market Funds or Treasuries. These count as 'Securities' ($500k limit) rather than cash.
  2. Download Statements: Once a quarter, download your PDF statement. This is your proof of ownership. If the app disappears, this document proves you owned 1,000 shares of Apple.
  3. Use Major Players: While startup apps are fun, there is safety in 'Too Big To Fail'. Fidelity and Schwab have trillions in assets. They aren't going anywhere.
  4. Direct Registration (DRS): For the paranoid, you can 'Direct Register' shares in your name with the transfer agent (e.g., Computershare). This removes the broker entirely, but makes selling harder.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is crypto SIPC insured?

No. Crypto held on exchanges (Coinbase) is generally uninsured. If they go bust (FTX), you are an unsecured creditor. You likely lose everything. Self-custody (Cold Wallet) is the only protection.

What about Money Market Funds?

They are securities, so they fall under the $500k SIPC limit, not the $250k cash limit. This makes them safer for large cash hoards than a bank account over the FDIC limit.

How long does it take to get money?

In a clean transfer (broker buyout), days. In a liquidation (SIPC claim), it can take 1-3 months. Keep an emergency fund at a separate bank just in case.
